speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Is Canada showing any specific interest in, or have we an observer at, the conference being held in London on the possibility of the British West Indies being federated and becoming a self-governing member of the commonwealth of nations? Is consideration being given to these islands joining Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CONFERENCE ON FEDERATION OF BRITISH WEST INDIES
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to give me notice of this question, which enables me to deal with it at once. We are continuing to follow very sympathetically the movement toward closer association of the British islands and territories in the Caribbean, with which we have had long and friendly relationships. We will be receiving reports on the conference which is now being held in London.
It should be made clear, however, that even if agreement is reached at that conference in London, ten legislatures will have to approve the final agreement before federation can be established. It may take as much as three years to accomplish these last steps. Even then the federation is not expected to be completely independent financially, as United Kingdom grants in aid will still be needed for some years. Therefore the movement toward complete self-government as a federated state will take some time.
So far as the second part of the question is concerned, the government has not given consideration to this matter.

speechtext:
The other day the hon. member for Eglinton asked the following question:
Has any application been received from the Russian government or the Russian ambassador for permission to open consulates across Canada? Has there been any expression of a desire in that respect?
If I might answer the second part of the question first, I may say that a year ago an official of the Soviet embassy intimated informally that his government might eventually request permission to open a consular office in Winnipeg or Toronto. However-and


this answers the first part of the hon. member's question-no formal request for a consulate in any Canadian city has since been made. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if the departmental egg inspectors work on the basis of secret instructions rather than according to printed regulations, as reported in the Western Producer of February 2, 1956?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO METHOD OF INSPECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was kind enough to send me a copy of his question. The reply is as follows. The report in the Western Producer of February 2, 1956, implies that secret instructions have been issued to the poultry production inspection staff in British Columbia, particularly with respect to the washing of eggs.
No such secret instructions have been issued. Some months ago the district officer of the poultry division of the federal Department of Agriculture in British Columbia advised the divisional headquarters in Ottawa that. it had been proposed that the department should, under their regulations, prohibit the washing of eggs sold as grade A-l. Federal regulations with respect to the grading of eggs make no reference to washing, and there is therefore no authority under these regulations to prohibit or otherwise deal with the washing of eggs. The district inspector in British Columbia was advised accordingly, and that he should not
Inquiries of the Ministry take any steps to prohibit the washing of grade A-l eggs. This was routine administrative procedure, and was no more secret than any other routine instructions issued to district inspectors.
I should point out, however, that the inspection of eggs in British Columbia or in any other province in Canada, in so far as it concerns eggs that are produced and sold within that province, is a provincial and not a federal responsibility. In some of the provinces they do require them to wash eggs, and in others they do not. The only position our inspectors would take with regard to it is that if eggs are being shipped into British Columbia from outside, or are being shipped from British Columbia to some other province or to the United States, then our inspector would have something to do with the inspection.
In order to overcome difficulties our inspector, when he inspects eggs that are produced and consumed in British Columbia, is operating for the provincial government of British Columbia. We have standing laws and regulations with regard to that matter. When the provincial inspector is inspecting eggs that go out of the province or come in from outside, he is acting for our department. So it would be impossible for any individual to know, without going into all the details, just which government the inspector was acting for at the time.

maintopic: PRICES PAID TO PRODUCERS IN RELATION TO FLOOR PRICE
speechtext: The floor that is set for eggs across Canada is an offer of the federal government to take delivery of eggs that are in storage as of December 1 in any particular year at a price of 38 cents delivered at the plant where they are stored. speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture in order to answer the requests of certain farmers. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is not necessarily any penalty. It is the general practice that when attention is called to anything which is considered irregular, it is corrected. However, in so far as those matters are concerned, I doubt very much if anyone in the house or outside it can determine whether or not a regulation has been broken when all you have is the actual price paid.
That is so because in some cases the individual trucks his own hogs to the centre where they are to be marketed. In many of these cases he takes them directly to the packing plant. He must take them to the stockyards if he is going to have them come under the floor price, but whether or not he takes them directly to the plant is a matter of his own choice.

made with the individual who sent the hogs. All these matters have to be checked before you can determine whether there has been any breach of the floor, and they are all carefully checked as soon as the individual sends in his sheet.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. It is obvious that the hon. member for Greenwood is not going to begin his remarks until some order has been established by the house, and I quite agree with the position he is taking. I think if every hon. member who initiates a debate at this time of day would take the same attitude the hon. member is now taking, we might perhaps have order right at the beginning of our discussion following the orders of the day.

Now that I have the opportunity I should like to make one further point. Would the hon. member for Greenwood please be seated while I do so. I wish to point out that too often standing order No. 12 is being disregarded. May I take this opportunity to ask hon. members to carefully study what standing order No. 12 says. I beg to draw your attention to paragraphs 3 and 4, and in particular paragraph 4, which says:
No member may pass between the Chair and the table, nor between the Chair and the mace when the mace has been taken oft the table by the Sergeant-at-Arms.
This is the point I am making further to that which I made a moment ago in asking hon. members to maintain order as soon as the discussion begins when the orders of the day are called. The calling of the orders of the day seems to be a general signal to promenade for far too many members. Often you see hon. members passing between the Chair and a member who has the floor, or circulating in other parts of the house. Certainly that is not good decorum, and I would ask hon. members to respect the letter of this standing order which has been placed there for a purpose. I would ask hon. members for their cooperation in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. It is my contention, Mr. Speaker, that under a ruling given by Mr. Speaker Sproule on February 13, 1913, in which he said that a motion must not raise a question substantially identical with one on which the house has given a decision in the same session, our present discussion is out of order. It is my contention that this house on February 1 of this session made a decision on a question which is identical to the one which is about to be debated this afternoon and which was debated yesterday. This was done on a recorded vote of 153 nays to 64 yeas. The amendment to which I refer as having been discussed in the house reads as follows:
In view of the present critical situation in the Middle East, this house expresses its strong disapproval-
These are the underlying words-
This house expresses its strong disapproval of the government's policy of authorizing the shipment of munitions of war to countries in that area not within the NATO alliance.
It is my opinion that the house made a definite decision and that the method by which the government determines its export of arms was decided by that vote. The amendment in relation to which discussion is taking place this afternoon reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this house, the procedure with respect to the issuing of permits for the export
Shipment of Arms Abroad of arms, ammunition, and military equipment, should be referred to the standing committee on external affairs-
If we have expressed an opinion on the method by which the government has been conducting its affairs with respect to the export' of munitions, I feel that we need not discuss the question further on a motion to go into supply, which has been preserved for hon. members to bring to the attention of the house matters that could not and would not come before the house under ordinary circumstances. This amendment concludes as follows:
-with instructions to consider and to recommend to this house a definite code of procedure with respect thereto.
I feel that this house has definitely recorded its opinion as to how affairs are conducted in respect to shipments of arms, and for that reason I maintain that this amendment is entirely out of order.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, may I say a word on the point of order. I observe that' the question as to order has not been raised from the government benches.
The hon. member for Kootenay East suggests in effect that these are similar motions. In my submission, Mr. Speaker, they are quite different and entirely dissimilar. My hon. friend has misread them or has misinformed himself in the course of reading them.
May I direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to precisely what the house decided on February 1. On a government motion that you leave the chair for the house to resolve itself intc committee of ways and means, the hon, member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbakeh on January 31 proposed the following amendment, to be found on page 724 of Hansard:
That all the words after "That" be deleted anc the following substituted therefor:
"in view of the present critical situation in the Middle East, this house expresses its strong disapproval of the government's policy of authorizing the shipment of munitions of war to countries ir that area not within the NATO alliance; and alsc condemns the government for the lack of candoui with which the matter has been dealt with in this house."
Later that afternoon the hon. member foi Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) introducec the following amendment to the amendmen' I have just read. It is to be found at pagt 728 of Hansard and reads as follows:
That the amendment be amended by inserting therein immediately after the word "alliance" thf following words:
"without at the same time making sure tha peace in that area would be guaranteed either bj

Shipment of Arms Abroad the United Nations or by the powers that signed the tripartite agreement of 1950, namely the United States, the United Kingdom and France.
Those two amendments were defeated on division in the house on Wednesday afternoon and those questions, of course, are therefore withdrawn from the subject matter of any other resolution or motion which may be introduced in the house at this session. No one questions that. However, in comparing those two amendments with the amendment now under debate you will see that they cover quite different subject matters.
I would draw your attention, sir, to the fact that the amendments introduced on January 31 were concerned with the policy of the government in reference to the shipment of arms; second, that the shipment of arms involved was to a particular area in the world. A third question was involved in the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Prince Albert, namely condemnation of the government for lack of candor. That has not arisen in the course of this present debate.
The amendment under debate today does not concern itself with the shipment of arms to the Middle East; it has to do with the shipment of arms anywhere. The amendment of last Tuesday, January 31, concerned itself with the policy of shipping arms to that particular area. The present motion has to do with the procedure to be followed in reference to the shipment of arms anywhere in the world.
Between the subject matters of those two motions there is a world of difference. However, it must be perfectly clear to hon. mem-oers that this present amendment has been Eramed having in mind the necessary acceptance of the fact that the question in regard :o policy as to shipments to the Middle East vas settled by the vote taken last Wednesday. The house decided last Wednesday that apparently it would not entertain a proposal disapproving of government policy permit-dng the shipment of arms to this troubled area. The present motion says in effect, "All * ight; that question has been decided. Apparently the policy is to permit the shipment >f arms. We will now go on from that point and concern ourselves with the question as ;o how those shipments are to be carried aut as a matter of procedure."
That involves the question of the issuance if permits; that involves the question of what 'overnment departments' are to be concerned n the issuance of permits; that involves the luestion of what knowledge parliament is to lave of the matter; that involves the question if government method in this matter, or


whether it is a matter of ministerial order or decision. It concerns the whole basis upon which these permits are to be issued.
That is quite a different field. This motion could not challenge the decision in reference to the policy that shipments of arms are to be permitted by government decision. But accepting that situation arising out of the defeat last Tuesday of the opposition amendment, this amendment goes on to say, "If shipments are going to go, it is time the house knew how"-you can spell "how" whichever way you wish-"they are to be made." This house must concern itself with the whole basis of the procedure in reference to such shipments. We are in a quite different field from that covered by the motion last week.
I point out that the subamendment introduced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar did not enlarge the scope of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert as I have just now discussed it.
I would also draw your attention to a very brief review of these decisions, including the one to which my hon. friend made reference, to indicate that there is no ground here for ruling out the present motion. In Beau-chesne's third edition, page 139, reference 357, we find the paragraph to which my hon. friend made reference. This contains a ruling by Mr. Speaker Sproule on February 13, 1913, which ruled out a proposed amendment on the ground that a motion must not raise a question substantially identical with one on which the house has given a decision in the same session.
I emphasize those words, "substantially identical". I have pointed out that far from being identical or even substantially identical, in this case the present motion is framed on the basis that the question as to policy in regard to the shipment of arms to the Middle East and Near East was decided by the house in rejecting last Wednesday the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Prince Albert on Tuesday.
Then if you will look at the notations on Speakers' decisions on pages 714 and 715 you will see that rulings in regard to matters that are substantially identical are not given lightly. On page 714 we have a decision by Mr. Speaker Smith on April 8, 1859, when he declined to rule out a later amendment simply on the grounds now put forward by my hon. friend because several additional particulars had been added to the former motion which was said to be substantially similar. Even the addition of several further particulars in that case was regarded as ground for holding that the two motions were not substantially identical.

Then on page 715 we have a decision by Mr. Speaker Cockburn given on April 3, 1871, when he ruled in effect that the amendment with which he was dealing related to an act which had already been before the house, had been reviewed by the house and had been the subject of amending legislation at the same session. The later amendment sought to be introduced de novo therefore was ruled out of order because the subject matter had been disposed of already. I have already made mention of the ruling of Mr. Speaker Smith where additional particulars were contained in an amendment.
It is quite obvious, I think, that we have here a clear distinction. The only possible effect of the amendment now under debate is that it does not attempt to reopen the decision made by the house last Wednesday on the amendment of the hon. member for Prince Albert. It goes into a new field. It accepts the decision made by the house and goes on to deal with a new question arising as a consequence of the decision of the house at that time.

Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious that the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has felt that this is at least a borderline case because apparently he has done considerable homework in order to counteract any arguments that might be made. The hon. member has suggested that this is an entirely new field. I was in the house for practically the whole debate, and I heard no new arguments. The whole debate revolved around whether we should or should not have shipped 15 or 25 unarmed planes to Egypt. The only change in the whole situation was the number of imbecilic stories through which I had to suffer.
Order.
I would draw your attention to the standing order dealing with irrelevancy or repetition in connection with amendments. If this amendment is not a repetition-

speechtext: Before I indulge in a speech on this point of order, would it be fair to ask Your Honour if there is any doubt at all about it? speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would say I have no doubt as to the position I want to take with respect to this matter. I do sympathize, however, with the point that has been raised. This I think, in fairness to the hon. member for Kootenay East, I must say because I have in mind at the moment a reasoning by Mr. Speaker Black with which I find a great deal of sympathy. He said that you cannot divorce a speech that is being made from the motion to which the speeches lead. This is why I stressed that point the other evening in the middle of the speech made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). If you speak in a certain direction and end in another, it is difficult to know exactly where the house is going, because the opener of the debate sets the pattern.
There is no doubt that the debate that tooK place the other day was on a motion to discuss external affairs. That was the intention, and the debate was arranged for that purpose. It was to be a wide debate on external affairs. Prior to the debate on external affairs the Secretary of State for External Affairs had made a speech during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, in which he said, as reported on page 463 of Hansard:
Now, what are the principles, the rules governing the shipment of military equipment from this country? These principles are the result of careful consideration and are, I think, sound and reasonable. The decisions based on them are made only after studying the relevant factors in every case submitted to us. The system of controls and checks through which policies and decisions are carried out is as effective as that of any other free country.
Then he dealt with the procedure, which is precisely what is being hit at the moment by the amendment moved to the motion that the Speaker leave the chair. It is the policy

Shipment of Arms Abroad referred to in that speech and the provisions made to carry out these policies that were hit by the motion of want of confidence moved the other day. So if the speeches are to be the same, leading to two different amendments, there is a good ground for the hon. member for Kootenay East to think that there is similarity between the two motions.
I am at the moment considering that a motion for the Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply is an opposition motion. It is one that gives the opposition great latitude, and I would not want to curtail the rights of the opposition in airing grievances. I would simply conclude this little argument by saying that the amendment is sufficiently different from that which was debated and decided upon the other day by the house, to be considered to be not substantially the same. I was not here last evening-as a matter of fact, I almost adjourned the house by mistake-but I do ask hon. members again, if they repeat arguments used in a former debate, not to make the same speeches which would have applied to the motion of want of confidence that was debated and defeated the other day. They should direct their speeches closely to the subject matter of the amendment they have moved, namely the procedure.
Some hon. members on both sides have referred to rulings that have been made, leaving perhaps the impression that the rulings made by former Speakers were proclaiming a doctrine that is new. It is the assertion of an old rule of parliament, which I find in Bourinot, fourth edition, page 328, and which reads as follows:
It is, however, an ancient rule of parliament that "no question or motion can regularly be offered if it is substantially the same with one on which the judgment of the house has already been expressed during the current session". The old rule of parliament reads: "That a question being once made, and carried in the affirmative or negative, cannot be questioned again, but must stand as a judgment of the house". Unless such a rule were in existence, the time of the house might be used in the discussion of motions of the same nature and contradictory decisions would be sometimes arrived at in the course of the same session.
Hon. members may consider too-and this is a point for future amendments which may be moved to motions that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply-that if the other day the house said that the policy of the government in dealing with this matter should not be condemned and if it decided today that the procedure under which they execute their policies should be condemned, then would we not have two contradictory decisions? It is a difficult point.


As I say, the motion in this instance is an opposition motion, and I would let the opposition benefit from the latitude which is usually given to motions of this kind.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in what you had to say about the promenade which usually takes place after the orders of the day. I would like to think that the rather larger numbers facing me today are due to a desire to hear what I am about to say. However I do not entirely believe it, because I think it has more to do with discipline than with any desire to hear me. It relates, no doubt, to a small incident the other day as a result of which I understand precautions have been taken so that it shall not occur again.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member at this moment is under the domination of a rule which says that, whenever he begins speaking, his remarks should be relevant to the question before the house.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
He needs discipline.

Mr. Speaker, I am venturing a short interlude in this debate because it seems to me, as far as my short experience of this house goes, rather unprecedented. I have often criticized the government before with a good heart, but I must say I never felt before that the government had made itself so supremely ridiculous as it has done in this case.
That is my excuse for being prepared to support the resolution that was laid before us, which makes a very simple suggestion, namely reference to a standing committee so that a definite code of procedure may be adopted.
It seems to me this thing has gone from bad to worse. Even today we are disappointed to learn that the undertaking that was given a short time ago is evidently now considered to be too comprehensive, and we understand from the Prime Minister today that it is being restricted.
Now that we have had a little look inside to see what happens, one begins to wonder whether this all-wise government does much of its other business in the same way. Why should it all be confined to the export of arms? Therefore I am proposing to discuss this resolution for a few minutes and try to assess the reasons, if there are any reasons, which the government might have for not adopting it.
I said last night that, so far as we could see from the evidence we had before us, in these series of occurrences the government has been proceeding by a kind of hodge-

podge of misunderstanding among two or three of its members. That is my justification. To me it is as clear as crystal. This is no ordinary matter. It is perfectly clear that this matter is affecting the conscience of the people of Canada, yet how was it dealt with by the government? It was dealt with in a routine way, as if it were supremely unimportant. I shall have a word to say about the famous order in council. I shall try to give a very short saga of the order in council which we discovered finally was not an order in council. It really seemed to evaporate into thin air.
At any rate it is perfectly clear, as I say, that there was bungling and confusion and anything but the kind of efficiency which this government likes to pretend it has. As I say, it was all treated casually. When I think about these 34 centres, sensitive centres I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) called them, and when I try to apply to them the reasoning the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) put forward last night, the vivid picture he gave of arms starting off in the casual way they do start, going off across the horizon to God knows where, and the utter impossibility of our being able to know what happens to them after that; when I think that might happen in literally dozens of cases throughout the world, I find myself extremely shocked. I also think a great many other people were shocked.
The other thing I want to know is how long this would have gone on. It was not found out by the government as such. It was found out by the opposition, by parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What was found out? Will my hon. friend tell us what was found out?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Not too much.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Make up your mind.

The shipment of these things we are talking about, the subject matter of the order in council which the minister told us the other day was not an order in council. It shrank during the course of its career in the House of Commons. I think we all know just what we are talking about, even though there has been a good deal of confusion about the matter. What a display this has been.
Although I am not an adherent of the government, I think I can honestly say I was shocked to find that a government, which after all is the only government we have, could do the things it has done and come here in a complete state of misapprehension among its various members, and then proceed
Shipment of Arms Abroad to sound off with really the most extraordinary series of mistakes. I would have thought that when this matter arose the government would have made very certain that there would not be any more mistakes made, and that there would be no further openings given to us.
I want to spend a moment or two, not long, in giving what I call the saga of this order in council, because I think it is very desirable for us to remind ourselves just what has happened. Then I propose to ask very briefly just what the reasons could be that the government would refuse to allow parliament to have a hand in the matter. If they will not it seems to me we may well wonder whether the legend on the labour publication the other day, which referred to parliament as one of the agencies of the government, was so wrong after all, and whether that is not the way they do regard parliament.
I want to give the saga of the order in council. On January 24 the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that the date of the order in council was July 7. On January 27 the order in council had a strange experience, because during the course of three hours it shrank. As appears at page 599 of Hansard of January 27, the Leader of the Opposition directed a question to the Prime Minister to which he answered as follows:
I shall see just what the order in council is and endeavour to have it available before the debate on external affairs.
Later that afternoon, as appears at page 639 of Hansard, the Minister of Trade and Commerce rose on a question of privilege and said:
... I should like to correct a misstatement I made through carelessness. I am reminded by a question addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this morning that on January 4-
I think it should be January 24.
-I referred to an order in council which conveyed approval of the shipment of Harvard training aircraft to the Middle East. I had in mind that orders in council were required for every export shipment, but that is not the case. They are required only in case government property is concerned. In the case of an export permit relating to private property, if it has anything to do with military affairs or if it is going to be a sensitive area-
One of the 34.
-ministerial concurrence is required by the ministers of external affairs, defence and trade and commerce.
Finally we have the death knell, as it were, of the order in council, at page 787 of Hansard. This was on February 2, two or three days later, when the Leader of the

Shipment of Arms Abroad Opposition again asked the Prime Minister about the order in council and the permit and the Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, that is a document which for other [DOT]easons it is not practicable to make public.
Later the Leader of the Opposition said: Mr. Speaker, may I then ask the Prime Minister what document there is that can be placed before the house which will show what actually took place on July 7?
The Prime Minister replied:
There is no document which can be placed before the house to show what actually took place on July 7. The hon. gentleman has been informed of how the matter was dealt with. It was dealt with by communications between ministers and those have invariably been regarded as confidential documents and have to be treated as confidential documents so that the ministers who are all jointly responsible for that which has been done, even under statute, by any one of them may see to it that they are properly informed of when and how they are going to have this joint responsibility.
In other words, as we see, in the course of about a week the order in council shrank into a permit, then it shrank into an understanding and then it really seemed to disappear into thin air. I think what happened is worthy of being compared with the writings of the author of "Alice in Wonderland". You remember these lines:
He thought he saw a banker's clerk descending from a bus.
He looked again and saw it was a hippopotamus.
Really it seems to me that this order in council, which has changed its character throughout, is almost worthy of being described in that way.
It started out as a hippopotamus.

What we are suggesting is a code of procedure. As I say, this is no ordinary business. This is a matter which touches the public conscience, and I think perhaps that is going to become more evident as time goes on. I should like to read a short extract from an editorial that appeared in the Toronto Star of January 28. It reads in part as follows:
In the present state of explosive tension in the Middle East, there can be no assurance whatever that the arms and equipment sent by Canada will not be used for aggressive purposes. Therefore, to ship arms there in any quantity or in any ratio is morally irresponsible: and it is inconsistent with a policy of promoting peace.
I quote again later-

speechtext: Is this the editor of the Toronto Star speaking? Are you reading from an editorial?
I am reading an editorial.

speechtext: Good. It is illegal, but go ahead.
Is that a ministerial order or an order in council?

Mr. Speaker, the acting speaker indicates that I may proceed. I continue:
A better way, we suggest, would be for the west to halt its arms shipments to the Israelis and Arabs, guarantee the existing frontiers against aggression by either side until a peace treaty can be signed, and back up the guarantee by placing international patrols in Palestine. This should be done through the United Nations if possible: and if that is not possible, it should be done by any combination of nations willing to take part.
The amendment has been put before the house as something which we are entitled to ask because of the unusual circumstances, because of the ineptitude which we have seen and which has shocked us, and because there is no sign that I can discern that the government is really going to change its ways.
I ask myself what reasons there are against the acceptance of this simple suggestion, namely reference to a committee to consider and to recommend to this house a definite code of procedure. There are two reasons which occur to me. The first is that there may be something more to be discovered, that there may be things which the government knows or suspects or fears. I do not want to think that at all; but if the matter is left as it is, I suggest that that consideration, that suspicion, that fear will remain. I think it will.
Surely the government does not suspect that in the plane which took the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) down to Rio there are any concealed machine guns, or that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), whose recovery we all hope for most sincerely, took a few rifle barrels down with him. Surely there is no fear of that kind. But that is one of the reasons which will be assigned if our suggestion is not followed. People will certainly ask, are there any skeletons in the cupboard? Of course when you find so many skeletons in one cupboard, you certainly may become suspicious of the others.
The other reason would be the one we know so well, namely that for the government to face the thought that parliament be allowed to take a part or to do anything is something they cannot do. It is just a thought which they cannot face. Here in July last there was an interlude in which certain things happened, and I think the Canadian people were interested. One might have thought that certain views might have been changed but I find little sign of that result.

Here is what I find about the Minister of Trade and Commerce. His feeling about what took place then was that we were just tiresome. If my memory serves me aright, at that time he said, as he listened to the speeches from this side of the house, that they seemed to him to come from some strange land. I hope I do not do injustice to his wording. I think I express what was in his mind. Then on January 16 last he said this, as reported at page 125 of Hansard:
What was the purpose of keeping us here during the month of July? It was to prevent the government from getting authority on a reasonably long-term basis to deal with the materials in short supply and to allocate those materials to the best advantage of the Canadian economy.
When I think of all the labour we devoted to the matter and all the instruction we gave to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I am disappointed that we made no greater impression than that; but there it is, and you must face the facts.
I think we must face the fact that the government may take the attitude which they so often have taken in the past, namely that to allow parliament to play any part in this matter is something that is just not done by well-regulated governments who have been in power for 20 years and who feel their oats.
The only thing I can do is suggest to the government that, just as happened last summer with respect to another matter, this matter is beginning to reach the public mind. I think there may be an increasing appreciation of the situation if it goes on, and I suggest to the government that as it was parliament-through the opposition-that brought this matter to light, and as it is parliament that is bringing it still further to light and is impressing it on the minds of the people of Canada, the people of Canada may well be surprised if the government takes the attitude that parliament may have nothing to do with this matter and says: We have blundered; we have been inept; we have been forgetful; we have been careless; we have been badly organized; nevertheless we are still the government and we are not going to allow parliament to have anything whatever to do with this matter.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to support this amendment I have in mind the remarks that have been made in this house today. I have no intention of describing incidents which have taken place in the past couple of weeks or even in the past couple of days. It seems to me that they are already on the record and there they will stand.
I might say that I approach this amendment with some diffidence because, as must
Shipment of Arms Abroad be apparent to all members of this house,
I certainly do not belong in the field of military experts. At a display of arms and munitions I confess to being somewhat awed. But I make no apology for that fact, because I believe that any ordinary citizen should be awed by the tremendous forces for human destruction which are today in the hands of men. I therefore speak today, Mr. Speaker, as an ordinary citizen concerned for the future of this nation and also for the sons and the young husbands and fathers who will inevitably be sent to defend us in the event that we should at any time find ourselves flung into war.
I do not want anyone to think for a moment that I am a pacifist; I am not. I am not an isolationist; I am far from it. Under NATO we are committed to co-operation with and support of our friends. As members of the British commonwealth of nations we are also committed to support the welfare of all the other members of the commonwealth. This is our family, and what involves them also involves us. However, when it comes to other countries I believe strongly that the sale of arms to small countries is not a deterrent to war. No, Mr. Speaker; I think the deterrent is in the knowledge that the great powers which are banded together in the United Nations will say no; and that not only will they say no but that they will back up what they say with action. Under the United Nations we are committed to trying to stop wars, not to fomenting them. I should like to read a couple of quotations from the preamble and the purposes of the United Nations as set out in the United Nations charter. At the beginning of the preamble we have these words:
We the peoples of the United Nations determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge oi war, which twice in our lifetime has broughi untold sorrow to mankind, . . .
Those are the very first words. I am one of those in this house old enough to have lived through two world wars. I know there are many hon. members in this house whc have not lived through two. There are alsc a great many who fought in two, and some who fought in the last one. To them I air sure a different picture must be presentee than that which is presented to me as ar individual who, because of my sex, was no' permitted to fight in either war as a direc combatant. However, there was no one whc stayed at home in those wars who did no do his or her part in some capacity or other So these words in this charter, Mr. Speaker touch our hearts as well as our intelligence

Shipment of Arms Abroad In the preamble it goes on to say, after citing the other determinations:
And for these ends,
to practice tolerance and live together in peace with one another as good neighbours, and to unite our strength to maintain international peace and security, and
to ensure, by the acceptance of principles and the institution of methods, that armed force shall not be used, save in the common interest, . . .
Yet we say to other countries, "Here are the weapons but do not use them"; or we say, "Here are the weapons and we will not look while you use them." Nothing here set out lends support to a policy of supplying arms, and certainly not to supplying arms to both sides in a controversy.
The purposes of the United Nations are outlined in the very first paragraph, which reads as follows:
To maintain international peace and security, and to that end to take effective collective measures for the prevention and removal of threats to the peace, and for the suppression of acts of aggression or other breaches of the peace, and to bring about by peaceful means, and in conformity with the principles of justice and international law, adjustment or settlement of international disputes or situations which might lead to a breach pf the peace.
As I said previously, Mr. Speaker, the greatest deterrent to war is the knowledge :hat the great powers will say no and will pack it up with action. Yesterday in this louse we had as a guest one of the greatest statesmen in the world, the Prime Minister )f the United Kingdom. Included in his renarks were some very pertinent comments. !e spoke about the last war, and how even vhen we were sure victory had been won here were still things that had to be accomplished. He made this statement:
He would still be a rash man or an ill-informed ine who would attempt a confident prophecy for nankind today.
I think that is what bothers all of us, the mcertainty. Where are we heading? What s in front of us? When even several mem->ers of the cabinet of one of the great nations if the world cannot agree as to what has aken place under their own jurisdiction, no vender the people of that nation feel some mcertainty as to their future.
After listing the various good points, as he ailed them, Sir Anthony had this to say bout the bad points or, as he called them, dose on the debit side. He said:
First, the increasing hazards which some are repared to take.
I hope we will digest those remarks of his, ecause in all the excitement of yesterday think possibly some of us were more con-erned with giving welcome to a welcome 

guest than we were with digesting his words. He listed the following:
First, the increasing hazards which some are prepared to take. Second, the dangers of aggression by countries which believe they can ignore the deterrent. Third, the continued existence of local disputes, whose consequences could engulf the world.
There were others, Mr. Speaker, but those three I should like to place on the record. It seems to me that the final one is the most dangerous of those three. It is dangerous because it could be built up on the first two. I do not believe for a moment that the people of this country get terribly excited about what happens a few thousand miles away if they think it is going to stay right there. But there is no power on earth that can draw a little line around a conflagration once it has started. There is no power that can say that when one tree in a forest catches fire the whole forest will not go; and that is what we are up against. How do we know that if a conflagration breaks out in some remote part of this earth today we will not be caught up in it before it is finished? We do not know. We are sitting on a keg of dynamite while the ministers of the crown throw lighted matches in a fine spirit of abandon.
If trouble breaks out somewhere, Canadian troops will inevitably be involved. If we are drawn into trouble, then this whole country will say to us, why did you not do something about this in the initial stages? Why did you not foresee that trouble would engulf us? Did you not live through two wars? Did you not see a minor incident in a remote country build itself into a war which engulfed all the peoples on this earth? Every member in this house, Mr. Speaker, represents thousands of citizens, and it is the duty of every member in this house to know what course we as a nation are going to follow. It is for that reason we think the matter of supplying arms and munitions should go to a committee where it could be properly assessed, a committee of experts on external affairs.
Yesterday in this house a statement was made by the Prime Minister with reference to the lifting of the embargo on the export of arms and munitions. Last evening, listening to the news on the radio, I cannot say I was surprised but I was interested to note that without exception the attitude taken by the newscasters was that this opened the gate again for a resumption of the activities which had been denounced in this house last week. Here we go all over again; more weapons to both sides.
We are bound on subjects of this sort, to obtain the considered opinion of a standing

committee of this house charged with the responsibility of delving into the pros and cons of each individual case as it comes up. I am agreed that each case must rest on its own merits, but the overall policy must be sound. Let us have no more of this trafficking in weapons; let us have no more of these invitations to war.
I said a few minutes ago that I was no pacifist and I am no isolationist. It is well known, Mr. Speaker, that I have always supported the defence preparedness of this nation and will continue to do so. I am satisfied to leave it to those who are experts in the field to determine what is adequate. I do not know whether or not the defences which we have today for Canada are adequate, and I should be talking nonsense if I attempted to establish myself as being knowledgeable on that subject.
However, it is my firm belief that we do not dare relax our preparations; we do not dare to let up in our efforts. It is also my belief that in the event we are drawn into war every able-bodied man and woman in this country must be available for the duties they are required to do, whether it be in the front lines or at home; and it is becoming increasingly apparent that these two posts of duty may very well be synonymous the next time a war occurs.
Therefore we must exercise care, Mr. Speaker. So we feel that these decisions must not be made in several departments of government without reference to other departments of government. We believe that anything as important as the export of arms and munitions must go to a place which will act as a clearing house for the various departments of government.
As I said, I believe we must be prepared, and I believe we cannot relax; but I object most vigorously to a slap-happy policy which makes of our people pawns in a game where the stakes are the lives of our young men.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my leader the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) indicated last evening, we shall support the amendment that is now before the house if a vote on that amendment should become necessary. It does seem to me that the government might even yet give favourable consideration to the idea of accepting this proposition without making it a matter of want of confidence. At the same time I should like to commend my friend and neighbour the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre for bringing this matter before the house in the terms in which his amendment has been drawn.
Shipment of Arms Abroad
I think we are all aware of the origins of the present discussion, and we are aware of the origins of this desire; nevertheless what is sought now is something totally different from what was under debate last week.
What is now sought is that permission be given to the standing committee on external affairs to review the whole question of the procedures that are employed in the issuing of export permits for munitions and materials of war. It is also suggested that that committee might be given the power to recommend a code which the government might in turn consider. I think it is obvious to all of us as the result of things that have happened in the house in the last two or three weeks that such a review is highly desirable, and I wish to commend our friends to the right, the hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party, on the excellent speeches they have made in connection with this matter.
I intend, Mr. Speaker, that my remarks in support of this amendment should be very brief. It is not my purpose to repeat the arguments that have been advanced by hon. members to my right or the arguments given last night by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. However, I do think emphasis might also be laid on the fact that not only is there a certain amount of uncertainty and bungling on the part of the government with respect to this matter which calls for a review, but it should also be remembered that there are certain private interests in the country which seem to have no objection to trafficking in the weapons and the materials of war.
We have been reminded during the discussions on this matter that there are two main categories of military equipment. There is that equipment which is in the possession of the services or the Department of National Defence, and there is also any equipment which commercial interests may have for sale to other countries. In addition to our concern as to the procedures with respect to war materials owned by the government or in the possession of the services, I think we should also be concerned as to the procedures by means of which permits are granted to private firms to export war materials of any kind to other nations.
In that connection I would remind hon. members that the morality of some corporations in a matter of this kind is not of the highest order, as was called to our attention back in 1943 in the case of Falconbridge Nickel Mines, Limited. Other hon. members who were here with some of us at that time may recall that on May 11, 1943, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar drew to the

The Minister of Finance is getting a bit ahead of me. He is perfectly right, it was condemned by everyone from the prime minister of the day down. But the point is, Mr. Speaker, that we should not forget that instances of this kind indicate the morality of some of these people.
Despite the interjection of the Minister of Finance I think hon. members should recall what it was the president of this company said to the shareholders of the company on that occasion. He had been discussing the position of the company's Norway refinery which was then in German hands. So far as the balance sheet of the company was concerned he said they might as well forget it for the time being, but he went on to say this:
Incidentally, you will be glad to learn-as I was-that through indirect channels it is reported that your Norway refinery is safe so far and is being maintained. It is in operation by your Norwegian staff, under German control, on the same Norwegian nickel-copper ore-production that we formerly handled on toll basis.
As the Minister of Finance has pointed out, once that statement was drawn to the attention of parliament by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar it was indeed strongly condemned by Mr. King and by others, for we all agreed that profits were hardly something to be glad about if it meant they were accumulated at the expense of material being used against our own troops overseas.
I should also like to remind hon. members of the statement which was made on September 12, 1939, by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, when there was a discussion about a certain limitation on profits. This is what the minister said, as recorded on page 179 of Hansard of September 12, 1939:
I can say to my hon. friend that from that day to this the defence purchasing board has done its very best to place contracts on that basis-
The basis referred to was the 5 per cent profit limitation.
-and has used every pressure that could be brought to bear in the form of patriotism and so on, but to date it has not succeeded in placing a single contract on that basis.
I know that statement has been argued backward and forward a good many times since, but there it was, an honest revelation by the minister of the experience which he


had had with certain profit-seeking interests in this country. I mention these two things, the Falconbridge statement in 1943 and the statement by the minister of munitions and supply, as he was then, in 1939, to indicate that the sinners in this matter of trafficking in weapons are not limited to ministers on the front benches opposite, but are also to be found among the ranks of the producers of war equipment.
Because there are these other interests, interests that think only of profit, interests glad to get orders anywhere in the world, I submit that for that reason, as well as because of the bungling we have seen on the part of the government since we came here for this session, it is time that the whole question of the procedures employed in the issuing of permits for the export of arms and ammunition should be reviewed by a committee of this house. Therefore we are glad to support the amendment which is now before us.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) indicated last night, we welcome this amendment. We feel that it is good and timely, because events of the last few weeks have indicated that there are severe weaknesses in the cabinet, that it is shot through with indecision and lack of co-operation. We certainly hope that the cabinet are not as loosely knit in all their other decisions as they have been in regard to shipments of arms to various parts of the world. There does not appear to be any co-ordination among departments, and one minister does not seem to know exactly what is going on in other departments even though the actions may be closely related.
As has been pointed out, not only has there been a lack of co-operation among various departments in this regard; the Prime Minister seemed to be completely at' sea as to what was going on. I quite agree with what the hon. member for Macleod said last night, that the opposition should not have to step into the breach and plug the holes caused by administrative blunders. I agree also with him when he says that when the government ceases to be able to govern, it is time to throw it out.
But we must stop to think and realize that we will not have an election coming up very soon. The government does have to run the country until an election is called. Therefore we will have to help to support them, we will have to put our arms around them and guide their faltering steps, until they can be replaced by an aroused Canadian people through an election.

I think we are somewhat similar to a sportsman out in the woods who finds that his boat has sprung a leak. He would like to buy another one, but until such time as he can get to a large centre he must simply plug up the hole and keep going. That is the position in which we find ourselves. It is the duty of all hon. members, including those of the opposition, to try to keep the government afloat and save the country from absolute ruin until such time as a competent government can be elected.
I was amazed at the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) interjecting in that regard, because he should remember how in 1952 and 1953 the Liberal government in British Columbia had taken the same attitude. They were thrown out hard and thrown out fast. As a matter of fact they were defeated so decisively and their morale was lowered to such an extent that they will not run candidates' in by-elections any more.
The proposal to send this matter to the committee on external affairs is I think good, and it should bring about a system of coordinated action as far as the government is concerned with regard to the shipment of arms. Then we in the opposition, as well as all hon. members, will be able to obtain some sort of coherent information when we ask questions in the house.
Although we agree with the amendment, I do not think 1 can agree wholeheartedly with the sentiment which provokes it. Several hon. members of the official opposition would seem to favour some degree of isolationism. As much as I dislike the thought of war-I do not want to go back again, and I do not want to see my children go to war-I cannot agree that our refusal to export arms is going to rectify the situation.
I do agree that there should be a great deal of thought and consideration before arms shipments are made to any part of the world, particularly to countries which are not our NATO allies. To be quite frank, I do not think the government has given proper consideration to the shipment of arms to countries throughout the world, but if we tie our hands so that we cannot make any arms shipments then we place ourselves in the position where we cannot ship arms to a country endangered by aggression.
We must remember that the iron curtain countries are shipping arms all over the world. They are gaining the favour of those countries by arms shipments, and if we refuse to ship arms we will only alienate the affections of a good part of the people of those countries. We simply cannot afford to do that. It would not be proper to permit the Soviet union to make arms shipments to certain
Shipment of Arms Abroad areas without making at least some attempt to maintain the status quo.
There is one more point in this regard I should like to deal with, one which I think is most important. If we tie ourselves down so we canot make arms shipments we may be laying a good part of the world open to communist aggression.
Speaking last evening the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) seemed to be highly indignant that other hon. members were not taking part in the debate. He seemed to indicate that they were the only ones willing to speak. I would remind the hon. member that they were in a position to go ahead and speak because they were in a position to be prepared. We in the other groups in the house had no idea of what was coming up, and we could not possibly be prepared. They had a veil of secrecy over the whole thing, the same veil of secrecy they seem to abhor in the Liberal government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You mean the Tories had the veil of secrecy?

That is right. They had as much secrecy about that motion as they seem to deplore in the Liberal government. I would certainly hope that air of secrecy would not be the attitude taken if we ever had a Tory government in Ottawa. I mention that only briefly because I do not think there is any possibility of that, so I shall not say any more about it.
As I said before, I can support the amendment because it gives us a chance to brace the weakening foundations of this government to the point where it may be able to stand upon its own feet until another election is called. However, I cannot support the sentiment attached to it, which appears to be isolation, as has been pointed out by the various speakers of the Tory party.

Mr. Speaker, I think the last statement of the previous speaker is undoubtedly off the beam. Certainly I do not think any member of the Conservative party is a pacifist or isolationist to any degree whatsoever. I have risen to speak on this motion because I feel the subject matter is of very great importance. There is a definite moral principle attached to it. Also I believe it is one of the most important subjects we have discussed since I came here in the fall of 1953. I would just like to read the motion:
That, in the opinion of this house, the procedure with respect to the issuing of permits for the export of arms, ammunition, and military equipment, should be referred to the standing committee on external affairs with instructions to consider and to recommend to this house a definite code of procedure with respect thereto.

Shipment of Arms Abroad
That is simple enough. It speaks for itself. It simply means that we are suggesting that this matter be discussed by the committee on external affairs and that it be given power to study and examine it from all angles and, having examined and studied the matter, it then brings a report back to the House of Commons.
To me there are two main questions involved. First, if we are going to traffic in arms, should we not know exactly what is going on and also exactly where it might lead? Second, it seems to me there is a question as to whether we should be in this deplorable business at all.
I do not propose to argue the factual or technical aspects of the debate. That has been done more capably than I can do it, by other members of my party much more equipped to talk on the subject in a detailed way than I am and with a world of experience. However, I cannot conceive of a more confused approach than has been taken by this government over the past weeks. What has been the attitude by this government in the past? They have given lip service to a role as peacemakers and go-betweens for quarrelling governments.
What do we find? The Secretary of State for External Affairs made a trip to Europe on a fact-finding basis, presumably a goodwill tour. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has been acting like a carpet-bag pedlar of munitions, willing to sell to practically any nation in the world. The Prime Minister says it is a competitive business. Is this not what some of the huge armament manufacturers have done in past years? Undoubtedly they have also in the past been responsible for starting wars; perhaps small conflagrations, but at the same time they have fomented strife simply to further assist in selling arms.
I wonder how many Canadians actually know what has been going on. I doubt if very many do. Quite frankly I know I had not realized, until this debate commenced, just what has been happening. As the hon. member for Hamilton West said a few moments ago, and I am repeating those words,
I am no pacifist, I am no isolationist; I am a Canadian first, last and always, but I certainly would like to know what is going on and whither it all may lead. The present policy of the government might well be thought to be gambling in lives-of the people of some other nation, possibly, but could it not eventually lead to Canada?
We are told that what is sold is scrap or so-called obsolete weapons. Why are we selling scrap? I am asking that question. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has remarked in this house that there is a shortage


of practically everything except wheat. Is there a shortage of steel? Why should we not keep this scrap in Canada? It could well be used here. Just how obsolete are the so-called obsolete weapons? In my estimation they are not obsolete to the people who are receiving them. Weapons can become obsolete only when they can be replaced with something better.
I feel the government's attitude must fall into one of three categories: first, acquiescence in the present hopeless position; second, shame at their mishandling of the whole business; third, outright alarm that at long last they have been found completely negligent.
I would like to know how this whole issue sits on the conscience of the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who have for so long posed as champions of peace. Has not this expose of government traffic in arms made a mockery, for instance, of our role at the United Nations? The United Nations is dedicated to peace. We have had disarmament conferences at the United Nations to talk peace. In my estimation we have been doing a great deal to foment trouble in various parts of the world.
Furthermore, Canada entered the North Atlantic Treaty Organization as a purely defensive alliance. Time and again, at home and abroad, government spokesmen have reiterated a Canadian policy of non-aggression. Now we find these are merely lofty sentiments. Apparently these sentiments are not to be allowed to interfere with what might be termed the cold practicality of turning what the government considers to be an honest dollar and which might well turn out to be blood money.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I am going to interrupt the hon. member for a moment and tell him quite frankly that he is causing me some embarrassment. I have no desire to interfere with the course of a debate which I know has been allowed to become fairly broad and which I take it should, in the opinion of the house, be allowed to become fairly broad, but I think the hon. member's remarks have brought me to the position where I must point out to him that the meat of the motion we are now discussing is that the procedure with respect to the issuing of permits for the export of arms should be referred to the standing committee on external affairs. Of course I have left out a lot of the words of the amendment.
In order to justify our right to debate that particular motion at this time it was pointed out at some length earlier this afternoon that what we are discussing is not-and I am using my own words-the morals or ethics or

lack of them in the exporting of arms but the question whether or not the procedures adopted by the government should be referred to a committee for investigation and recommendation. I am going to ask the hon. member and those who will be following him to try to direct their remarks largely to that question because, as was pointed out from this rostrum earlier today, otherwise we are going to have, if not in resolution at least in debate, a complete repetition of what we had last week. I feel quite sure the hon. member for Perth and others realize the difficulty in which that puts the Chair and will do their best to assist us.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not wish to put you in any difficulty. That would be the farthest thing from my mind. However, I feel quite strongly about this matter, and my reason for approaching it in this way is to try to show that there are reasons of humanity across the whole world why it should be referred to the committee on external affairs.
As I mentioned at the outset of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I am going to be brief and I am not going to deal with the technical or factual side of the question as I consider others to be more capable of doing so than myself. But I should simply like to say that there is either a right side or a wrong side. If we are on the right side it must be uncompromisingly so. If we are wrong, then I think our policy should be changed. How can we find out except by referring the matter to the committee on external affairs? If we do not do this, it seems to me it will be a downright shame for Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address myself rather briefly to the amendment before the house.
How about wheat?

You will hear plenty about wheat. The amendment calls for referring this matter to the external affairs committee for the purpose of establishing a procedure. Two things that are rather noticeable have been missing from the debate up to this point. One is the fact that no member of the government nor, as far as I am aware, any member of the party supporting the government, has had anything whatever to say on the amendment.
We decided the question last week.

That makes it rather difficult to know just what the intention of the government is with respect to the amendment, whether they intend to sit out the R7509-59
Shipment of Arms Abroad debate, assume that the amendment is a straight matter of want of confidence and treat it as such or whether they would prefer on this occasion to treat it on its merits.
The leader of this group has placed on the record the attitude of our party. We are supporting the amendment in the hope that it will bring about a method by which members of the house, and in that way the public, can become better informed as to what is being done and how shipments of arms abroad are made. That is the reason why it would be very valuable if some member of the government were to take part in the debate and set qut the attitude of the government. If they feel the amendment is not justified, then there has certainly been plenty of time in which they could have so informed the house and stated their reasons therefor. The silence of the government indicates that either they are supremely disinterested in the question as such or they have no defence whatever to offer, and I hope it will soon become clear which one of these reasons prevails.
In my opinion the other thing that is lacking so far is that while the amendment calls for referring the question to a committee for the purpose of setting up a code of procedure, so far as I am aware not one member of the official opposition has yet stated just what procedure or method they would like to adopt. It is easy enough to call for a code of procedure, but I think the house and the country deserve a more explicit statement of what is in the minds of those who have moved the amendment.
It is quite clear they have nothing in mind.

That of course puts them right in line with government policy. I have a proposal to make which I hope will commend itself to the members of the Progressive Conservative group, my friends to the left and perhaps even to the members of the government. If we are going to exercise public control over the export of arms, and it is understood that we are now referring to arms shipments to other than NATO or commonwealth countries, then I think the best way to do it would be to set up a crown company which would be charged with the responsibility of being the clearing house for this type of export. The crown company should be responsible to parliament, report to parliament through a minister, and report to a committee. Unless something of that nature is set up then I am afraid we would not be very far ahead if the government, for example, were to say that they were quite prepared to let the members of the external
930	HOUSE OF
Shipment of Arms Abroad affairs committee ask questions about the issuing of export permits and so on but of course they would guarantee no answers. That type of thing has happened before.
As a matter of fact it was the subject of a motion on the part of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) last year when he complained bitterly about some of the things that went on in the estimates committee where ministers of the government either were members of the committee or took the attitude that their officials could answer only those questions which the minister concerned permitted them to answer. Therefore unless some clearly established machinery is set up through which all these procedures can be channelled in a responsible manner, and unless such an organization can be made responsible to parliament as a whole, I doubt very much if we will be very much farther ahead than we are at the present time. There are good reasons why there should be a public clearing house such as a crown company for the purpose of keeping strict public control over arms shipments outside of the NATO and commonwealth countries.
Reference has been made in this debate- mostly by interjection-from the other side to the fact that the amounts, the volume or the value of the arms shipments made to date in recent years has not been large. In relation to our war expenditures or our defence expenditures, that statement certainly is true. The amount of $20,000 or $1,500 or $30,000 or half a million dollars in relation to the total defence expenditures or the war expenditures during the war is a small amount of money. But the principle that is involved, as I understand the present procedure, is this. It is not too easy to understand, I may say, because we get a great variety of explanations, and then explanations of explanations, when ministers are questioned. But as I understand the matter up to this point the procedure is this. Again may I say that I would appreciate it if a member of the government were to enter this debate and make a clear-cut explanation of what actually is being done. But as I understand it, what is being done now is that a private firm may come to the government, and not necessarily to the government as such but to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) or to some official of that department, because we know that responsibility is delegated down the line. It might be the fifth assistant of the third deputy who receives the application for a permit for the export of certain arms to a certain country by that private firm. We have not yet been told just what is done or what investigation is made at that point as 

to the propriety of the export of those arms; as to the effects it may have on our international policy; or as to the effects it may have on the possibility of an arms race among various countries in a certain part of the world.
We do not know-we are not told and we are not able to find out; in fact we are as much as told that it is not any of our business-what procedure is followed to investigate and to determine whether such a permit should be issued. We know that certain permits are issued. We are not told-and we cannot find out at the present time-whether these firms that apply for these permits for the export of arms have any international connections in their business. We know that in the past it has been the case. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) recalled to the house, even during the time when Canada was at war we know that certain of these firms had international connections which, even in time of war, found themselves on the other side of the fence doing business. But even in peace time do we know whether some of these firms have international business connections, whether they have particular private interests to protect which are not combined with the public interest of Canada or with the national interests of Canada or of the commonwealth. All these things have a bearing on what is done.
For example, we do not want private firms to be profiteering at the expense of human life and property, whether it be in Canada or elsewhere; nor do we want international business connections to become privateers in the business of arms regardless of what effect it may have upon Canada or upon Canada's friends and international relations. These are things that need to be found out and I can conceive of no better way at the moment. If someone has a better suggestion I should like to hear it. Certainly, unless I have not heard correctly, I have not heard a definite proposal made by any member of the Progressive Conservative group as to what they have to recommend with respect to a clearing house procedure if this matter was referred to a committee and if the committee gave this matter consideration.
My proposal is that a crown company should be set up, that that company should be responsible to parliament as a whole, and that it should be the agency, under the control of parliament, which should determine in which cases export permits may be issued if it is in the best interests of this country that this should be done; and there conceivably are cases where it may be in the interests of this country that export permits should be issued. But that is a matter that should

be considered on the basis of public interest and of the national interest of this country and not in the interests of any private group who are out to profiteer or to a privateer in an arms race.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who preceded me has just drawn attention to the fact that we have not yet had any statement of the government's position in this matter. Quite apart from the question that fact raises as to whether the government-including the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin)- has anything in mind, it might be regarded as somewhat of an insult to the house that a serious suggestion put forward in a field which is of such grave concern to the people of Canada should receive from the government no statement as to their position.

Under the terms of the motion moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), we are discussing a suggestion that the procedures governing the issuance of permits for the export of munitions of war should be referred to the standing committee on external affairs. I refer particularly to the statement issued by the United States government when they turned down an application for the export of $50 million worth of munitions to Israel. The other factor which indicates there is an urgent need for a review of policy in this field is a statement made yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as recorded on page 880 of Hansard, when he answered a question asked earlier by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).
