Mr. Speaker, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) calls for two things. First, that a committee investigate the shipment of arms which has taken place and, second, that the committee recommend a code to govern such shipments and procedures in connection with them in the future. I submit that those two proposals are eminently reasonable.
Surely parliament is entitled to know exactly what has been done in this matter up to date and what will be done in the future, particularly the policy and the procedures that will be followed from now on as far as the shipment of arms is concerned. Certainly we do not know at the moment either of these things. The whole matter has been a picture of confusion ever since the beginning of this session of parliament. We had a series of statements by ministers, each one amending or correcting what the previous statement had said. It was quite evident that the ministers directly concerned with this matter, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of National Defence, just did not know what happened. Apparently they did not know what policy, if any, was being followed, and, particularly, the way in which it can be carried out. Thus it is quite apparent that the cabinet as a whole was just not in the picture as far as arms shipments are concerned.
When we come to parliament and the Canadian people, nothing was known of these arms shipments. It came as a shock to me, and I think to most of us here and also, I am sure, to most Canadians, to learn that we have been shipping arms to the Middle East, the very area where there is and has been


for some months past the greatest fear of a war breaking out. It was a further surprise to all of us to find we had been shipping arms for several years past to Central and South America. I do not think that many Canadians relish at all the idea of Canada being in the arms business. I am sure all of our citizens want to be assured that, to the extent that we are in this arms business, the strictest supervision and control is exercised in the sending of arms abroad.
As a result, I am quite sure that a committee such as that proposed and a definite code coming out of that committee, to govern all arms shipments, would be generally welcomed throughout Canada.
The Prime Minister's statement yesterday that the embargo on the shipment of arms has been lifted returns the situation to the same unsatisfactory state it was in before the question was raised. I would just like to read part of the Prime Minister's statement and comment upon it. He said, as indicated on page 880 of Hansard:
. . . the embargo is now to be lifted at once. The government intends to continue the policy which has been in force of considering each application for military equipment on its merits and ensuring that if permission is granted it shall, in the future as in the past, be for military equipment of a type and quantity which could not provoke an arms race or provide an incentive to aggression.
How can the Prime Minister or any of the other ministers, or the cabinet as a whole, determine what type and what quantity of munitions is going to provoke an arms race or is going to be an incentive to aggression? I do not think it is possible. As has been pointed out previously, many conflagrations start from very small sparks. The first great war started from the murder of an Austrian archduke, and I am quite sure that when that murder took place very few people thought it would develop into a world war. Similarly it is not possible, in my opinion, for the Prime Minister or anyone else to say that a batch of arms or a group of ammunition is not going to be an incentive to aggression and is not going to provoke an arms race.
It brings up what some people seem to consider a distinction between defensive and offensive arms. Personally, I do not think there is any distinction. I have heard some people arguing that some or most of the arms we sent abroad were defensive arms and not of an offensive nature. Arms of any sort are offensive in the general sense of the term and in the sense of the term that they can be used to mount an attack, that is, the strictly military use of the term "offensive". I seems to me that, no matter what sort of arms you export, you are putting into

the hands of the people who get those arms the capability of mounting an attack, of starting an aggression. You cannot distinguish as between types of arms. In that regard, I suppose many people might consider anti-aircraft guns as purely defensive arms. However, during the last war-particularly during the last year of that war-the heavy ack-ack guns of our army fired a greater number of rounds in the ground role, and certainly not in a defensive role, than they fired at aircraft. They were extremely good medium guns when used in ground actions. Therefore you cannot class any of these weapons as purely defensive arms. They are all offensive; and they can all start trouble.
There is another facet of this matter which makes the reference of it to a committee very desirable. What I refer to is that it involves the cost to the Canadian taxpayer of the arms and ammunition which have been shipped abroad. I do not refer here to the arms shipped to other members of the commonwealth and to members of NATO. We have shipped large numbers of arms to the NATO countries as part of our commitment to that organization. Whether we should have shipped some of those arms or whether it would have been better to have kept them at home is a matter of defence policy, but those are not the arms I refer to. However, it is a very pertinent matter for this parliament to know to what extent arms shipped to countries other than the commonwealth and NATO countries have been subsidized out of public funds.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) yesterday outlined how upwards of a million dollars' worth of guns, rifles and ammunition have been shipped to Central and South America during the past eight years. The question immediately comes to mind:	Was this material
manufactured by private firms on a commercial basis, such as the commercial transactions about which we have heard, or was it government stocks which held been disposed of as surplus to requirements? It would not imperil the security of the Israeli government or anybody else's security. It is a financial fact that the house should know. From looking at the list and knowing only a little about what the cost of some of these items was during the war, I strongly suspect that all this equipment has been sold at a fraction of its cost to the taxpayers of this country.
It is all very well for one of the ministers to get up now or at a subsequent time and say that the 3 [DOT] 7 heavy ack-ack gun is obsolescent. It may be obsolescent but we have nothing to replace it. Every time we ship a 3 [DOT] 7 ack-ack gun out of this country we leave a blank in our defences and so far we have nothing with which to fill it. Although it may be obsolescent it can still have quite a deterrent effect. It seems to me that- the whole policy of shipping guns out of the country without having something with which to replace them is a matter which should come under review and needs such a review in very quick order.
The same thing applies to the 25-pounder gun. There are many gunners who would say that these guns are equal, if not superior, to the United States 105 millimetre which is replacing them at the present time at very great cost. In any event, we have shipped a large number of 25-pounder guns chiefly to our NATO allies, and to my knowledge we have not received any guns to replace them. The result is that another blank has been left as far as our artillery situation is concerned. That is a further matter which should be investigated. I think it certainly requires investigation.
The general position is that we are getting rid of equipment which cost us very large sums of money at very low prices and without getting anything to replace it. As a result we are leaving ourselves short. As has been suggested by others in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the government will accept the suggestion put forward in the amendment and refer the whole matter to the external affairs committee or some other committee for investigation and report.

speechtext: Quite a case has been built up, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of rather flimsy evidence indeed. When is scrap metal mutilated and when is it not mutilated? The hon. gentleman said: "Yes, it might apply to breech blocks but what I am interested in is gun barrels", whereas the minister's reply-as he will see if he will read it again-referred to guns themselves, not to any particular parts. It seems ridiculous, Mr. Speaker, to build up a case to such a high moral and emotional level on evidence of that kind.
The hon. gentleman also made great play with the fact that I and others on this side of the house did not realize that conventional weapons are modern and dangerous. Of course we realize that a conventional weapon can be both modern and dangerous. As I
have often said-and it is an obvious truism_
you can be killed by an old-fashioned bullet as well as by a new-fashioned atomic bomb. But that is not the point, Mr. Speaker. Hon. gentlemen opposite are criticizing us because we are adding to tension, are producing incentives to aggression, are causing trouble, are losing our reputation in the world, and are being toppled from our moral position. As was said by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) this afternoon-if I may be pardoned a personal reference-my own reputation as a peacemaker has now been sullied because we have sent to friendly countries, under control, some old surplus conventional weapons, small in quantity and really not very important in quality. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, who is the sponsor of this amendment, said this, as reported at page 887 of Hansard:
What in the world has happened to the millions of rounds of ammunition sent down to Central America, the Caribbean and South America? . . . Then what is going to be the outcome of this reckless disregard, as it appears to me, in handling that type of equipment?
He even went so far as to suggest that we were responsible for the revolution in Guatemala. In a few moments I shall come to the details of the shipment to Guatemala which produced the communist revolution. He also suggested that we might have had something to do with the overthrow of the government in Cuba in the few thousand dollars' worth of ammunition that went to that country; and $800,000 worth of ammunition and equipment, as he called it, that has gone to the Latin American countries in the last eight years. That was the type of thing that he put on the record. I should like later to examine in some detail one particular shipment to which he referred.
He referred first to my statement, recorded at page 557 of Hansard, that no permits were issued in 1954 or 1955 for the export of:
. . . guns, ammunition, or military weapons of any kind, or for military aircraft or military vehicles to South America.
He suggested that by a careful midnight examination of his own he had found that I had incorrectly represented the situation, and thereby must have misled the house. My original statement, Mr. Speaker-and it has been checked-is perfectly correct. No such permits were issued. Earlier in the session- and I commend this to the hon. gentleman who might refresh his memory by reading some of these back statements-I referred to the list issued in accordance with the provisions of the Export and Import Permits Act, items subject to export control. That was the heading under which I gave my figures. The

hon. gentleman has shown a great deal of industry in examining the export statistics by the dominion bureau of statistics, whereas if he had come to me I would have given him the original material on which I based my answer to the house, in all of its detail, and he could have checked it against any public or private source. I should have thought that he would have considered it worth while in the course of his research to look at the control list; arms solely for sporting purposes-and this is in the control list- firing ammunition not usable in firearms designed or intended for war are clearly exempted. He could have found that out. Perhaps he did find it out and it escaped his memory before he made this statement. The various shipments to Latin American countries to which the hon. member referred, and by doing so gave the impression to the house that they had been omitted by me in my statement to the house, fell in this category. They consisted of 22 calibre rifles, shot guns, revolvers and ammunition for them.
Let me remind the house, Mr. Speaker, that such sporting weapons and ammunition for them are freely available for private purchase in shops throughout Canada. The total annual trade in such ammunition for such weapons within Canada alone is of the order of $10 million a year. A single Canadian firm does an annual business in such ammunition within Canada of some $5,800,000 a year. That, Mr. Speaker, is the perspective within which we should look at the figure of $64,000 of such items shipped within a two-year period to four different countries in South America, and over which the opposition has become so very indignant; over which they have condemned the moral standards of the government, and as the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has just said, have provided the incentive to aggression.
The hon. member, throughout his remarks, returned several times, and I have mentioned this earlier, to the suggestion that the government was concealing information on this matter. I should like to remind him now, and others who have spoken on this matter, that the exemption of sporting weapons from export permits requirements appears in regulations published almost two years ago, regulations which in fact were brought to the attention of the house two weeks ago. Furthermore, the shipments of such items that have been made appear regularly in separate figures issued by the bureau of statistics. No doubt that is where my hon. friend got this hair-raising information.
The hon. member has, in fact, himself demonstrated that this information is readily
Shipment of Arms Abroad available. It is public now. My only comment on his activities is that in his haste to put these supposedly damaging figures before the house he appears to have overlooked one additional item for $155 for Venezuela in 1955.
Well, Mr. Speaker, so much for that information and so much for the deductions which have been drawn from it that we have been responsible for all sorts of dire happenings in the central and south American area, especially in Guatemala, where there was of course a little difficulty a few years ago. The hon. member referred to that.
Under a communist controlled government.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The shipments to which he referred, to Guatemala, were in this same category, ammunition suitable only for small arms designed solely for sporting purposes. They consisted mainly of 22-calibre ammunition but some shotgun ammunition and revolver ammunition was also included. No guns of any kind were involved. These items, Mr. Speaker, were consigned by the firm in question to a Guatemalan sporting club. There is no reason to suppose that they were used for anything else than target shooting at clay pigeons. The amounts involved were small by any standards or else we might have had some reason to get suspicious of them if they were very large in amount, because you can do damage in any country even with ammunition designed to shoot clay pigeons. But in relation to the quantities of ammunition shipped, it is ridiculous to suggest that these shipments could have contributed to maintaining in power the communist infiltrated government which was replaced in July, I think, of the following year.
It is that kind of argument, Mr. Speaker, and the deductions that have been drawn from it which leads some of us on this side to wonder about the motives of the opposition in raising this matter in the way they have raised it, at a time when we are discussing with our friends in Washington, our friends in London and our friends in Paris, how best we may work together in contributing to peace, not only in the areas of the Middle East but in the other areas of the world. Only in the last few days in these discussions we have been going over the question of arms shipments to sensitive areas, especially to the Middle East. It may not have escaped the notice of hon. members that the Secretary of State of the United States this morning has reaffirmed, after the discussions which took place in Washington between representatives of the United Kingdom and the United States, that he on behalf of his government

Shipment of Arms Abroad was going to maintain the present policy and principles in the declaration of 1950. He did not intend to depart from that policy because, as was indicated, a departure from that policy would have had most unfortunate consequences in the Middle East in respect of one country at least which is not in a position to get help from behind the iron curtain that certain other countries in that area are now getting. The United Kingdom, Mr. Speaker, intends to maintain that policy, too. We, in this government, intend to maintain the same policy, and work it out in co-operation with our friends and under controls at home.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) who moved the amendment said that some of this ammunition might eventually get into the hands of the Mau Mau. I suggest that so far this ammunition has only gotten into the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite, where it is being used not with an effect that I would describe as lethal but rather as a soporific. I believe, of course, that arms policy and arms shipments are perfectly legitimate subjects to discuss. But so far, we have heard a great deal more about arms procedure than we have heard about arms policy from hon. gentlemen opposite. I must say, however, that they have, in some of the statements made from the opposition side, made their position pretty clear in regard to their refusal to send any arms except to the commonwealth countries and the NATO countries with which we have a definite military alliance.
We will continue to follow the policy that has been outlined previously, and to follow it in a way which will not be conducive to aggression or conflict but which might help, by the way it is controlled, to preserve peace by removing the temptation to an aggressor to attack an unarmed country opposite or close by. There is no greater temptation to aggression than the certainty of an easy victory. A policy, if it were adopted by all free countries, of refusing to send any arms to any country except under the conditions which have been outlined by hon. members opposite, would leave some countries weak and defenceless, and other countries which did not have any scruples about receiving arms from behind the iron curtain in a position to attack those countries. If we had followed ths policy, we might very soon have cause to regret it.
My final word, Mr. Speaker, is that the committee on external affairs will be set up very shortly. As is customary, I expect to appear before that committee. I will be very happy, as usual, to subject myself to crossexamination as complete as hon. members


opposite would like to make it in respect of any sphere of my activities, arms policy or anything else.

Of course, most hon. members in this house know that sporting weapons can be pretty deadly; -303 Enfield rifles, Colt, Smith and Wesson and British Webley revolvers are not ordinarily regarded as sporting equipment but they are offered duty free under the benign arrangements made by this government.
This is the kind of subject we want to have come before a committee. We want to find out exactly what is being done. Let us now examine the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in discussing this subject. He pooh-poohed the suggestion that there was any importance to this; he indicated they were just unimportant little shipments,-these -303 Enfield rifles, Colt, Smith and Wesson and British Webley

Mr. Speaker, I have drawn attention in times past to the dangers of monopoly particularly in reference to the media for the communication of ideas. Likewise, attention has been drawn on more than one occasion by those who sit in this part of the house to the danger of attempted government control of the means of expression, especially when that control is directed to serving partisan purposes. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation claims to operate free of government control. The time has come, sir, to examine such claims and also at the same time to examine the definition of some of the terms that have been used in this regard.
Last autumn there was published a volume entitled, "The Age of Mackenzie King". The authors of that work are Bernard Ostry and H. S. Ferns, two eminent Canadian scholars now on the staff of the University of Birmingham. To say the least, the book was not complimentary to the late Mr. Mackenzie King or to the record of the Liberal party before and during the period of his leadership. Indeed, the book has gone some distance to explode some of the myths which the Liberal party has sought to create. The book has, therefore, become a controversial book.

speechtext:
I wish at this time to draw to the attention of the house some of the unfair labour practices engaged

in by the government of Canada. I do so as a result of several questions asked with regard to the post office department since this session commenced, and which were asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and myself with respect to the liquidation of overtime accumulated during the Christmas rush. As a result of the answers given by the Postmaster General at that time I am wondering whether we realize the seriousness of the government's attitude towards the problem of the 40-hour week and the whole question of overtime. At the time the bill to increase postal rates was before the house we were told it would be necessary to increase the postal rates in order to take care of the additional costs of instituting the 40-hour week and the wage increases involved.
During the course of that debate many of us wondered just how clear the government was in its understanding of the 40-hour week. I recall asking the Postmaster General at that time if he was aware of the fact that the normal practice for a 40-hour week was to pay time and a half for all time worked in excess of the 40 hours. At that time he replied that the government policy was to give the workers a 40-hour week and if they worked over 40 hours they would then be paid at their regular rates of pay. As a matter of fact, it was much worse than that at the time. We were told that the regular postmen who agreed to work a sixth day would be paid at the rate offered to temporary or casual help, which would mean in effect that they would be working at a rate less than their regular rate of pay. Then, after a great deal of confusion on the part of the minister, we did get the impression that the government policy in this regard was to require that the employees work 40 hours and then to ask them if they would work a sixth day. They went much further than that, too. There were complaints coming to hon. members from postal groups throughout the country referring to the efforts made on the part of the postmasters to get personnel to work six days; and mark this, while they were supposed to be working a 40-hour week they were asked to go back and work six days at their regular rates of pay. The government could see nothing wrong with that at the time. I think that is a clear indication that this government has no concept of what the 40-hour week really is.
There were several other matters which entered into the discussion at this time and these matters were brought up at a later time when the estimates of the Postmaster General were before the house. I am not going to refer to them except to state that the pattern indicates the lamentable record
Post Office Department-Labour Relations of the government in its relations with its employees. We were happy that the government backed down in connection with the question of the priority of holidays which would have been destroyed to a large extent by a change in regulations.
Not long ago the government proposed to introduce penalties for those who were late in arriving at work, and we remember the tremendous outcry which quite naturally arose from those who were affected. Hon. members in this house indicated the folly of that plan, an insult to a loyal group of public servants.
A short while ago the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) brought up the question of the installation of television in the post office in Peterborough. It is quite true that the government has not talked about putting television in any other post office but we are led to believe that this is more or less an experiment and if the government is satisfied with it then I presume there will be a movement to instal television in other post offices across Canada.
Each of these instances is serious enough in itself but when you see the over-all pattern indicating the callous disregard on the part of the government for the rights of public servants in this country we realize that the government should undertake a revision of their entire attitude.
While we are talking about the dismal record and maladministration on the part of the Post Office Department we must mention the latest instance, which has to do with the liquidation of Christmas overtime. I received, Mr. Speaker, a copy of a resolution passed at the January meeting of the Regina branch of the Canadian postal employees association and I should like to read the resolution because I think it clearly outlines the legitimate complaints of these postal workers:
Whereas-
During the Christmas rush, postal workers are called on to work 14 hours per diem (less lunch periods) in order to process the tremendous amount of extra mail to ensure delivery before the holiday.
And whereas-
Workers are put to additional expense for extra meals and for taxies.
And whereas-
Four extra hours are worked per week before time and one half is paid,
Therefore we of the Regina Branch of the Canadian Postal Employees Association do unanimously protest the recent ruling of the Post Office Department to liquidate some of this overtime during the month of January.
When this question was raised in the house the Postmaster General made the most amazing statement. He said that there is nothing wrong with this because this is the practice throughout the civil service. In other words,

Post Office Department-Labour Relations crime is not important if it has become compounded. The fact that this is the practice throughout the civil service is a poor excuse for treating the post office employees in this shameful manner.
The minister made another amazing statement when he said there is an order in council which covers the question of overtime. Well, who passed the order in council? How can the government hide behind an order in council on a matter of this kind? The government passed the order in council stipulating that overtime would not be paid under certain circumstances but instead this time would be liquidated during the month of January.
My contention is simple: If the government could pass an order in council restricting and impeding rights of postal workers, then the same government can rescind that order, in council and treat the postal workers properly. If the minister considers that because this is common practice throughout the civil service it is an excuse for the poor treatment of one group of civil servants, then I suggest it is time the government reviewed the system. I should state, Mr. Speaker, that while I am giving a specific instance concerning the Post Office Department I am by no means suggesting that the Postmaster General is more at fault than is any other member of the government. This is a decision which has been made by this government and the Postmaster General is apparently carrying out the government's policy in this regard. It is that government policy which I am protesting at this time.
I think we have to be quite clear that a 40-hour week means that the workers work 40 hours and every hour worked in addition to the 40 hours is overtime and must be paid for at overtime rates of pay. I think we have to recognize that the payment of overtime rates is not a question of incentive to the employee. In reality, overtime rates of pay are a penalty against the employer. A great many unions forbid their members to work overtime because they realize that many employers use overtime as a means of keeping their labour force at the irreducible minimum and that if overtime were not paid the labour force would have to be increased.
Moreover, if there are employees who are not averse to working overtime I suggest it is because their rates of pay are so low they are compelled to accept overtime as a means of supplementing their income and the answer to that is simply not working more overtime but paying more adequate rates of wages.
I have stated before in this house that the government of this country ought to be setting an example to all other employers in Canada

but instead of that we find departments of this government which have established the reputation of being the worst employers in Canada as far as treatment of their employees is concerned.
I ask this question: How many employers in this country could get away with what the Post Office Department apparently got away with this year? I wonder how many packing houses or how many factories could say to their men around Christmas, "We are awfully busy this year and are going to require you to work many hours in excess of the regular work week; if you work you can take time off in January." They would not get away with it; there is not a trade union in this country which would put up with it for a moment, and yet civil servants of this government are being obliged to put up with that sort of thing.
I make the plea to the government at this time that they give serious consideration to this matter and recognize their responsibility to the people of this country and that they ought to be setting a good example to other employers rather than setting a bad example. They can set a good example by taking into consideration all the aspects of the 40-hour week and doing away with unfair labour practices which have given the government a black eye as far as their relationship with their employees is concerned.
I say to the Postmaster General (Mr. Lapointe) and through him to the government:	Now is the time to pay heed to the
representations that have been made. I do not know what the Postmaster General and other ministers of the crown do when representations are received. I have read the resolution passed by the branch in my constituency and I think it indicates to hon. members the reasonableness of the request these people are making. They are not asking for anything which any employee in this country has not the right to get.
What is the government going to do about it instead of getting up and saying they are not going to do anything in connection with this department because it would affect other departments. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) stood up in this house last year when the post office estimates were being considered and said that they did not want to discuss this matter at that time because it had to do with the civil service commission and the civil service as a whole.
I am not levelling my criticism at the Postmaster General alone. I ask him and his colleagues in the government to give active consideration to the request made by these

public servants and usher in a new and better concept of labour relations in the government service.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the subject raised by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis). I have had occasion before to speak in regard to this matter for certain civil servants. I think the time is long past when any branch of the government of Canada should adhere to the old method of asking workers to work overtime for the privilege of taking time off a little later. As far as the post office employees are concerned they are glad to do this and are ready to work overtime at a time of the year when most people like to have time with their families. But when they do this they are asked to take time off at a period in the year when there is not much else they can do except to sit at home. Surely this government is advanced enough to get away from that old way of treating employees.
I am not going to say much more in this connection. I think all that needs to be done is to draw to the attention of the government how obsolete this sort of treatment is and to ask the government to treat the civil service on the same basis as the employees of private industry are treated. Times have changed in the last few years as far as the relations of workers and employers in industry are concerned. The workers are no longer standing in daily fear of what may happen to them in their employment. They have developed organizations and are thus able to demand consideration from their employers which they never would get without such organizations.
I have not the press clipping with me but since coming down here I read an article in a paper published in Quebec-I think the incident occurred in that province-dealing with the prosecution of some employers in the lumbering industry for cruelty to the horses used in their operations. The judge was quite scathing in his remarks and he said something like this: The workers in industry have organized and can demand proper working conditions, but the horses are not in a position where they can organize, and when cases of this kind are brought before them the courts should see that animals are treated properly. I intended to bring that clipping down with me and I probably should have it, but I left it on my desk.
That brought home to me the fact that only a few years ago the workers in this industry had just as little to say about the conditions under which they had to work as the horses had. But things have changed. I suggest
Post Office Department-Labour Relations to the Postmaster General (Mr. Lapointe) that he discuss this matter with his administrative staff and I think they will soon realize how old-fashioned it is to say to an employee, "The circumstances are such that we want you to work overtime for the next two or three weeks and then a few weeks later you can take time off as we will not need your services then".
A worker should be paid for his services. If he works overtime he should receive a higher income. When he receives that higher income he should be able to do with it what he likes and in his own time and not be at the beck and call of his employer, whether that employer be the government of Canada or private industry.

Mr. Speaker, I have spoken privately to the minsters about this matter of post office employees, as well as hourly-rated employees in the national parks. I think these two matters are sufficiently related to justify their being dealt with at this time. I feel I should express my appreciation to the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) for having brought forward this matter, and indicate that I intend to support him in his contention that an employee, whether working for the government or for industry, should have equal rights and privileges. When it is impractical or impossible to carry out the amount of extra work in a post office during the Christmas rush, it is the normal practice to hire temporary employees, but it would seem that they are not extending this practice sufficiently far to provide for all the extra work that is required. Therefore the regular employees are required to work overtime during the Christmas rush and then take time off when they are not required. A more orderly consideration should be given at the outset to this, and if we have enough employees on regular employment that it would cause no dislocation to have them take time off during the work week, then we are not making the best use of our regular employees. If they are required to work overtime, in the province, particularly, where the work week is defined, they should not be expected to work in excess of that work week without some compensation. I do not believe that the compensation is set down in the actual statutes. They simply state the work week as so many hours. Usually the employees make their own arrangements with the employer as to what compensation shall be paid. Certainly overtime is not straight time at regular rates. They should be compensated at rates higher than the regular rates when required to work over the eight hours or over the 40-hour or 44-hour week, as the case may be.

Pensions for Disabled Persons
The other question with which I am concerned is the matter of day rate employees working in the national parks. Those who are in the civil service have their regular work week set down by the civil service commission; and in many cases' it is eight hours less per week than their fellow employees working almost side by side with them. The civil service employees will be able to call it a week on Friday evening in many cases, while the day rate employees must continue to work on through Saturday and very often at a lower rate of pay. We understand, of course, that in such services as are provided in national parks Saturday and Sunday work must be carried on. I thought I should bring that matter also to the attention of the minister.

Furthermore, there should be a waiting room where we can receive and greet people who come to see us as members of parliament. Something should be done now to remove the bad impression which this House of Commons gives the people of Canada when they come to visit us. People must be made to respect this house and honour the noble traditions of democratic government. Not one person in ten who visits here leaves without an impression of having been let down.
The tragedy of Canada is that our people do not realize how indifferently, how inadequately and how badly we, the Canadian people, are governed. The government-financed Liberal propaganda machine has, by hollering loud and long and by dint of repetition, lulled far itoo many Canadians into believing that all is well and that this country may continue in this slap-happy, indolent method of government while we struggle with only a small part of the Canadian heritage which would be ours if we had in Canada a progressive wide-awake government, which only the Conservative party can provide.
I was forcibly reminded of this during the recent by-election campaign when the real issues were brought before a people that had hitherto placed its confidence in the Liberal party. If the Canadian people knew the facts they would resolve never to vote for this government again. In the time of the late Mackenzie King it was government on the advice received at seance meetings through these professional mediums, of dead people and dead dogs. Of course those were the days before high fidelity and the late prime minister is reported having complained that the voices from the grave were often scratchy. Of course he never bothered to look under the draped tables in these

Income Tax-Pension Funds seance meetings to see the old gramophone which brought him these dead voices.

My remarks will only be of a few minutes' duration. I should like to say that I believe a great many people are concerned about the future of the C.B.C. They see something that is good in the C.B.C. We must keep the C.B.C.
As I said in the first instance, my criticisms are based on the proposition that we must not have any government interference that might result in the misuse of that organization. I would say that until the government has cleared up this question doubt and suspicion will remain in the minds of a great many people that this public institution is being misused by this government in order to keep from the people what would appear to be something that was not in the interests of the Liberal party. I do not think that is good.
I hope, therefore, that the minister is able to clear the C.B.C. on that score.

There are only a few minutes remaining, but I should like to state a matter of privilege. It seems to me that when time is limited under our new rules for a certain debate, perhaps some arrangement might be made where there could be a more equitable distribution of the time between the various parties in the house. Now you will notice perhaps my point of privilege when I explain that a debate took 
place the other day wherein the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) spoke twice to the exclusion of even permitting another group to mention why they were going to vote in a certain way on the amendment. All day yesterday and today we debated an amendment to the motion that you leave the chair. The Leader of the Opposition and many others spoke on that motion. Now, that was in the form of a grievance.
As soon as that motion was disposed of a member of the same party rose to take the floor. Perhaps he had a right to do it, but he spoke on the same subject on which the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) asked a question today. Perhaps he would have followed that with his grievance if the next party in line had obtained the floor. It simply means this, Mr. Speaker, that there should be some gentlemanly agreement and fairness in the distribution of time. It does seem to me that when one party leaves off, at least the other party should be able to follow. After that, I am not too concerned. Much of that responsibility, I think, rests with our Conservative friends. If they expect all parties to be fair they had better be fair now because they may not be sitting in that preferred position after the next election.
So say you.

They will look to others who are in that position to be fair. I mention this as a point of privilege, and I think when it is considered perhaps all will agree that my point of privilege is fairly well taken.

On a question of privilege,
I should like to point out for the information of the hon. member that in speaking tonight after the vote on the amendment I was speaking for the first time in this debate. As to the second point, his suggestion that the matter I was discussing had been raised by way of a question by another hon. member,
I may tell him that I also was concerned in that matter. He apparently was not in the house to hear me say that I had intended to ask a similar question and did ask a question this afternoon. I had also informed the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort that I intended to raise this question here tonight. There was no intention on his part to raise it, as he indicated to me at that time, so there is no ground for any suggestion that any member was prevented from raising the same question I raised here tonight.

speechtext:
As the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) has said, it is a matter that hon. members could well either discuss amongst themselves through the usual channels in order to arrive at some understanding or else if an hon. member

believes that the member taking the floor should not be doing so he can always move a motion that must be put without debate, that is that the hon. member be now heard. Standing order No. 29 reads:
When two or more members rise to speak, Mr. Speaker calls upon the member who first rose in his place; but a motion may be made that any member who has risen "be now heard", or "do now speak", which motion shall be forthwith put without debate.
I will do my best to distribute the time as fairly as possible, but as I say the house can always take care of the matter because by virtue of the standing order I have just quoted it is in their own hands.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
